extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in discrete mathematics / proof-based mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and exercises about binary relation properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, antisymmetric), partial and total orders, extremal elements (smallest/minimal/largest/maximal), bounds (upper/lower, l.u.b./g.l.b.), closures, and how these properties behave under set-operations and relation-composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is reflexive if ∀x ∈ A (x R x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflexivity is preserved by adding the identity relation: the reflexive closure of R is R ∪ i_A. Example: L = {(x,y) ∈ R×R | x ≤ y} is reflexive. To prove reflexivity for composition: if R and S are reflexive then R ◦ S is reflexive (exercise 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is symmetric iff ∀x ∈ A ∀y ∈ A (x R y → y R x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition of symmetric relations need not be symmetric in general; for R and S symmetric, R ◦ S is symmetric iff R ◦ S = S ◦ R (exercise 17). Use counterexamples to show naive inheritance can fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is transitive iff ∀x ∈ A ∀y ∈ A ∀z ∈ A ((x R y ∧ y R z) → x R z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitivity can fail to carry over under certain constructions on P(A) depending on quantifier structure (see exercises 19–21). If R and S are transitive then R ◦ S need not be transitive unless additional inclusion conditions hold; e.g., if S ◦ R ⊆ R ◦ S and R and S are transitive then R ◦ S is transitive (exercise 18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antisymmetric relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.1: R is antisymmetric if ∀x ∈ A ∀y ∈ A ((x R y ∧ y R x) → x = y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to capture 'at least as large as' notions where equality is forced when both directions hold. Examples: L = ≤ and S = ⊆ are antisymmetric. Antisymmetry together with reflexivity and transitivity defines a partial order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial order
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.2: R is a partial order on A if it is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial orders model comparisons that need not compare every pair. Examples: subset relation on P(A) and divisibility on Z+ are partial orders. Verify each of the three properties when checking whether a relation is a partial order. Intersection of partial orders (on same A) preserves the three properties (exercise 6a / exercise 5 shows restriction to B × B preserves partial-order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Total order
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.2: A total order is a partial order with ∀x ∈ A ∀y ∈ A (x R y ∨ y R x) (comparability for every pair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total orders compare every pair (e.g., ≤ on R). A partial order need not be total (⊆ on P(A) is not total). If R is a total order then many minimal/smallest relationships simplify (Theorem 4.4.6(3): in a total order, minimal implies smallest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest (R-smallest) element of B
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.4: b ∈ B is an R-smallest element of B iff ∀x ∈ B (b R x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a smallest element exists it is unique (Theorem 4.4.6(1)). A smallest element is also minimal and the only minimal element (Theorem 4.4.6(2)). In subset partial order, being smallest means being a subset of every element of the family (e.g., {2,3} smallest element of family F in Example 4.4.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal (R-minimal) element of B
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.4: b ∈ B is R-minimal iff ¬∃x ∈ B (x R b ∧ x ≠ b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal elements need not be unique and need not be smallest. Provide counterexamples (Example C with two minimal elements but no smallest). In a total order any minimal element is smallest (Theorem 4.4.6(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Largest element of B
rubrics_metrics.description: b ∈ B is the largest element of B iff ∀x ∈ B (x R b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Largest elements are unique and imply maximal; the analogous dual statements to smallest/minimal hold (see exercises 14 and 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal element of B
rubrics_metrics.description: b ∈ B is maximal iff ¬∃x ∈ B (b R x ∧ b ≠ x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximal elements are dual to minimal elements; a largest element is maximal and unique (exercise 16). There can be multiple maximal elements when no largest exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound for B
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.8: a ∈ A is a lower bound for B ⊆ A iff ∀x ∈ B (a R x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lower bound need not be in B (difference from smallest). Example: 7 is a lower bound for C = {x | x > 7} but not a smallest element of C because 7 ∉ C. The set of all lower bounds may have a largest element (g.l.b.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper bound for B
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.8: a ∈ A is an upper bound for B iff ∀x ∈ B (x R a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upper bounds may exist without a least upper bound (l.u.b.) in general posets; e.g., words example where two minimal upper bounds preclude a least upper bound (Example 4.4.10(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Least upper bound (l.u.b.) / greatest lower bound (g.l.b.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.4.9: If U is the set of upper bounds of B and U has a smallest element then that element is the l.u.b. of B. If L is the set of lower bounds and L has a largest element then that element is the g.l.b. of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence of l.u.b./g.l.b. is not guaranteed in arbitrary partial orders (special properties needed, e.g., completeness of R). In P(A) with subset order, l.u.b. = union and g.l.b. = intersection when the family is nonempty (Theorem 4.4.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Least upper bound and greatest lower bound in subset order
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 4.4.11: For nonempty F ⊆ P(A), the least upper bound of F (in the subset partial order) is ⋃F and the greatest lower bound is ⋂F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires F ≠ ∅. Proofs use subset relations and minimality arguments; exercise 23 asks to prove the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive closure of a relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 4.5.1 & Theorem 4.5.2: The reflexive closure S of R is the smallest S ⊆ A×A such that R ⊆ S and S is reflexive. Concretely S = R ∪ i_A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show S is reflexive closure, verify (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S is reflexive (i_A ⊆ S), and (3) minimality: any reflexive T with R ⊆ T must contain S. The closure is unique when it exists (Theorem 4.3.6). Example: closure of proper subset relation is subset relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of composition with respect to reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Various exercises/theorems: if R and S are reflexive then R ◦ S is reflexive (exercise 16). If R and S are symmetric then R ◦ S is symmetric iff R ◦ S = S ◦ R (exercise *17). If R and S are transitive and S ◦ R ⊆ R ◦ S then R ◦ S is transitive (exercise 18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition can preserve, fail to preserve, or require extra conditions for property inheritance. Use explicit proofs or counterexamples depending on property and hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with induced relations on P(A) (existential vs universal quantifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several putative constructions: S = {(X,Y) | ∃x ∈ X ∃y ∈ Y (x R y)}; S = {(X,Y) | ∀x ∈ X ∀y ∈ Y (x R y)} (with B excluding ∅); S = {(X,Y) | ∀x ∈ X ∃y ∈ Y (x R y)}. The exercises ask which of reflexive/symmetric/transitive are preserved from R to these S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quantifier structure matters: existence-based definitions need not preserve transitivity (exercise 19 asks to locate the flaw and provide counterexample). Universal definitions can preserve transitivity if empty sets are handled properly (exercise *20 shows excluding ∅ is necessary). Mixed quantifiers (∀x ∃y...) produce different inheritance behavior; check each property separately and give counterexamples when false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric + transitive does not imply reflexive (proof-checking heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Putative theorem and 'proof' that assumed existence of y with x R y when x is arbitrary: the proof is flawed because it presumes for arbitrary x there is a y with x R y. Symmetry and transitivity alone do not force reflexivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proofs, check hidden existential assumptions. Provide counterexamples (e.g., the empty relation on a nonempty set is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive) to show the theorem is false as stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection and union behavior for partial orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises 6 and 7 probe whether R1 ∩ R2 or R1 ∪ R2 must be partial orders when R1 and R2 are partial orders (on same or disjoint domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersection of partial orders on the same set preserves reflexivity, transitivity, and antisymmetry (so R1 ∩ R2 is a partial order). Union need not be a partial order in general, but if domains are disjoint R1 ∪ R2 is a partial order on A1 ∪ A2 (exercise 7a). Adding A1 × A2 to the union can make it a partial order (exercise 7b). Provide counterexamples to show failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation preserves partial order property
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 13: If R is a partial order on A then R^{-1} is also a partial order on A. Dual statements hold: largest ↔ smallest, maximal ↔ minimal under inversion (exercise 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check each defining property under inversion: reflexivity and antisymmetry are symmetric under inversion, and transitivity of R implies transitivity of R^{-1}. Use these to transform extremal-element statements by replacing R with R^{-1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness and implication relations among extremal notions (Theorem 4.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 4.4.6: (1) If B has a smallest element, it is unique. (2) If b is smallest then b is minimal and the only minimal element. (3) If R is a total order and b is minimal then b is smallest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategies: instantiate universal definitions with the candidate elements, use antisymmetry to derive equality, use proof by cases when totality causes pairwise comparability. These facts are standard checks when reasoning about minimal/smallest elements.
